2. The official challenge validator checks both inputs, including regulation names and versions when the regulation index is supplied.

description: rules pick the regulations, BM25+ (bigrams) ranks their clauses from spec queries, cite the top 190 clauses (no LLM)
explain: The same checklist picks the rulebooks (4 of 55). Then the search engine scores each individual rule (each numbered paragraph) by how many words it shares with the product description, and the 190 best-matching rules are handed in. It is the simplest baseline: fast and free. Its weakness is that word matching misses rules written in different words and includes rules that only sound similar.
explain_technical:
1. Regulation selection: `regselect` `combined` (rules + supersession + vehicle-category filters): R48, R148, R150, R10.
2. Corpus: `data-ingestion/clauses` of the selected regulations, one chunk per clause (multi-page clauses cited at their first page), regulation title prefixed.
3. Queries: `spec_queries()` (about 25, from `spec.md`); retriever BM25+ (k1 1.2, b 0.75, delta 1) on unigrams + bigrams; per-query top 400 fused with reciprocal rank fusion (k0 60).
4. Output: top 190 clauses with paragraph (190 = dev gold size, declared in `risk.json`).
5. Dev: page P 0.32 / R 0.60 / F2 0.511, clause F2 0.148, regulation F2 1.0.
risk_flags: regulation rules written by looking at the dev product (generic families, but only one case to test them); submission size N=190 equals the dev gold size
risk_notes: Retrieval baseline; regulation selection is the main dev-specific risk.

description: rules pick the regulations, then Claude (opus 5.5) keeps or drops each of their 'shall' clauses; every kept clause is cited
explain: Picture the 55 UN Regulations as a library of rulebooks. First a simple checklist reads the product description (lamps, a reflector, LEDs on a circuit board) and picks the rulebooks that apply: here 4 of the 55. Then Claude reads every sentence in those 4 rulebooks that says something "shall" be done (about 1,200 of them) and answers one question for each: does this rule apply to our rear lamp, yes or no? Every "yes" is handed in as a requirement, with the page and paragraph it came from. It finds almost every right page, but it also says "yes" to some rules the experts did not list.
explain_technical:
1. Regulation selection: `regselect` method `combined`: about 35 regex rules map spec terms to regulation families, then a supersession filter (R148 / R149 / R150 list the regulations they consolidate in their introduction) and a vehicle-category filter from each regulation's paragraph 1 scope. Dev: R48, R148, R150, R10.
2. Candidates: every clause of those regulations in `data-ingestion/clauses` matching `\b(shall|must)\b` (1,240 on dev).
3. Classifier: `claude-opus-5-5`, effort medium, structured output (JSON schema `{id, applies}`), batches of 40 clauses (text cut at 900 characters) with the full spec and an include / exclude rubric, 6 parallel requests, cached per batch.
4. Output: every `applies = true` clause as one requirement (clause text, first page, normalised paragraph); no ranking and no size cut (308 on dev).
5. Dev: page P 0.54 / R 0.98 / F2 0.844, clause F2 0.619, regulation F2 1.0. Overfit risk medium: the rules and the rubric were written while looking at the dev product.
risk_flags: regulation rules written by looking at the dev product; classifier prompt lists clause kinds seen in the dev gold (marking, photometry, installation, EMC)
risk_notes: No size cut-off and a generic prompt, so less fitted than the retrieval variants; LLM answers vary run to run (cached per batch).

description: rules pick the regulations, BM25+ (bigrams) ranks whole PDF pages from spec queries, cite the top 150 pages (no LLM)
explain: The same checklist picks the rulebooks (4 of 55). Then a search engine, a smarter Ctrl+F that scores how well the words of a page match the words of the product description, ranks every page of those rulebooks. The 150 best-matching pages are handed in. No AI reads anything, so it is free and gives the same answer every time. But matching words cannot tell which rules really apply, and the number 150 was chosen by trying sizes on the practice case, so it may not carry over to a new product.
explain_technical:
1. Regulation selection: `regselect` `combined` (rules + supersession + vehicle-category filters): R48, R148, R150, R10.
2. Corpus: own PyMuPDF parser, one chunk per PDF page of the selected regulations, regulation title prefixed.
3. Queries: `spec_queries()` builds about 25 from `spec.md` (product, functions, parts, material rows, part x product, whole spec).
4. Retriever: BM25+ (k1 1.2, b 0.75, delta 1) over unigrams + bigrams with stop words removed; each query's top 400 fused with reciprocal rank fusion (k0 60).
5. Output: top N = 150 pages, one requirement per page, no paragraph. N chosen by `export --sweep` on dev (F2 peak), hence overfit risk high. Dev: page P 0.28 / R 0.79 / F2 0.580, clause F2 0 (no paragraphs).
risk_flags: N=150 picked by a size sweep scored against the dev gold; regulation rules written by looking at the dev product
risk_notes: The size cut-off is fitted to the only labelled case; expect a lower score on the held-out case.

description: No-training BM25 + dense retrieval, 32 source packets, Claude extraction and source-aware review
explain: Claude first reads the product description and picture and writes down what the product is and what to look for. It skims the first pages of every rulebook and drops the ones that clearly do not apply. Two kinds of search then find the most relevant pages: one matches exact words, the other matches meaning (so 'braking light' can find 'stop lamp'). It also follows pages that those pages refer to, up to 32 bundles of 3 pages. Claude reads those pages carefully and writes each obligation as its own requirement, quoting the source, and a checker confirms every quote is really on the cited page.
explain_source: Drafted by Devansh's Claude from Jojo's README; Jojo, please check or replace with your own EXPLAIN.md.
explain_technical:
1. Claude reads the specification and product image, recording facts, unknowns and search queries.
2. A shared scope pass examines the title and first three pages of every base regulation. Clearly incompatible regulations are excluded; conditional and uncertain ones are retained.
3. Union the top six BM25 and dense hits for each generated product query; follow resolved references to depth two and inspect at most 32 three-page packets, including opening pages of retained regulations. Deferred pages remain explicitly unreviewed.
4. Claude reads full source text, governing ancestor clauses and original images of main pages. Every machine-detected candidate must receive an included/excluded/unresolved decision.
5. The runner verifies candidate coverage, source pages and verbatim text quotes. One repair call is allowed for structural/evidence errors. It deduplicates identical text and reviews applicability, conditions and duplicates in batches of 35 requirements. If the cost ceiling stops review, remaining drafts are marked unresolved and excluded from submission.
6. The official validator and base-page checks run before the submission is frozen by SHA-256.
Both variants use the same prompts, source corpus and model (`claude-sonnet-5-5`). Dense retrieval uses local CPU `BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5` with FastEmbed 0.7.4, 384-dimensional normalized vectors and cosine similarity. BM25 uses SQLite FTS5. There is **no weight fitting, no training and no RRF in this pipeline**. The included standalone retrieval module exposes additional experiments; its fitting command is not called.
risk_flags: Generic ancestor-context and conditional-applicability prompts revised after inspecting development-case source/output errors; no fitting to gold scores.
risk_notes: Only one known development product. The 32-packet limit was chosen before scoring solely to meet the user-authorized USD 12 total spending ceiling, not by a score sweep. Gold is read only by the separate benchmark after the submission is frozen. The cost ceiling also limited final review; unchecked drafts are excluded without consulting gold.

description: Exact Flat cosine scan of all BGE vectors + Claude source review (32 packets)
explain: Like the targeted version, Claude first describes the product and skims each rulebook. The search here uses only meaning: every passage of every rulebook is turned into a list of numbers that captures what it means, and each search question is compared with all 31,000 of them, with no shortcuts, to find the closest ones. The best pages (up to 32 bundles of 3 pages) go to Claude, which reads them and writes requirements backed by quotes. It is a clean baseline to see how far pure meaning-search gets on its own.
explain_source: Drafted by Devansh's Claude from Jojo's README; Jojo, please check or replace with your own EXPLAIN.md.
explain_technical:
1. Freeze the product specification, product image and source corpus fingerprints.
2. Claude profiles the product and assesses each regulation using its opening pages.
3. Encode the profile's search queries with the existing local BGE-small-en-v1.5 encoder. Anthropic is used for interpretation and generation; BGE supplies vectors.
4. Compute cosine similarity against **all 31,056 normalized, 384-dimensional vectors**, in blocks of 8,192. The matrix occupies 47,702,016 bytes. Scope filtering happens after the full scan. Sort exactly, breaking ties by corpus order, and deduplicate clause windows before taking six clauses per query.
5. Merge query results round-robin, follow source references to depth two, and select up to 32 three-page packets, including opening pages and governing context.
6. Claude reads source text and PDF page images, extracts obligations, checks applicability/evidence and reviews duplicates. Unreviewed candidates and unresolved references remain explicit. Freeze the schema-validated predictions before scoring.
7. Run the unchanged TL repository citation benchmark and regenerate dashboard rows.
The inherited hybrid retriever already calculated dense dot products exhaustively. This experiment makes Flat a standalone retriever, removes lexical scoring entirely, and scans all vectors before scope filtering. It is **not** an HNSW-versus-Flat speed comparison. Round-robin query merging also differs from the original BM25+dense workflow's sequential union, so end-to-end differences do not isolate index type.
The extraction model is `claude-sonnet-5-5`. Exact model-file hashes, Python and NumPy versions are in `retrieval-verification.json`; pinned dependencies are included. Flat retrieval has no random sampling. LLM generation is not deterministic.
risk_flags: Inherits an existing workflow developed on this product; no Flat parameter sweep or score-based selection.
risk_notes: One known development case only. Gold used only after frozen predictions in the official benchmark. 32 source packets fixed for comparison and cost.

description: SPLADE++ + BGE dense RRF, MiniLM cross-encoder top 200, Claude evidence-based requirement extraction
explain: The input is a product specification, its drawing and the supplied regulation PDFs. Claude turns the specification into search questions, then two local search methods find passages by related words and by meaning. A smaller model orders the strongest matches, and the workflow adds neighboring pages and referenced rules. Claude reads those sources, writes requirements with quotations and checks whether each requirement applies to the product. The output contains 395 retained requirements with citations; uncertain decisions and unread sources stay visible in separate reports. The main weakness is incomplete coverage, and the search settings were selected using one known product, so the measured result may not transfer to another product.
explain_technical:
1. Freeze the product specification, image and corpus hashes.
2. Search version-scoped text windows with local SPLADE++ and BGE-small-en-v1.5.
3. Fuse the two rankings using equal-weight RRF, k=60; deduplicate clause windows.
4. Optionally rerank a bounded head using MS-MARCO MiniLM-L6, preserving the tail.
5. Merge product queries round-robin, expand source references and attach PDF images, neighboring pages and governing section context.
6. Claude checks applicability, conditions, evidence and duplicate candidates; mechanical validators check the result. Unreviewed sources remain explicit.
7. Freeze predictions before running the repository's unchanged benchmark.
`config.json` records the selected development configuration. `selection.json` records its selection rule: page Recall@100, then nDCG@100 on the single development case. `retrieval-comparison.json` contains all compared variants. This is exploratory selection, not held-out performance. The internal leaderboard measures citations, not semantic requirement accuracy. Cross-encoder scores never exclude obligations.
risk_flags: Query strategy, candidate-pool size and optional reranking head selected by a development Recall@100/nDCG@100 sweep on the single labelled rear-lamp case
risk_notes: Indexing, query planning and requirement generation never read gold answers. Gold page labels are used by the separate retrieval evaluator to select configuration. This is exploratory development performance, not held-out generalization. Claude generates and reviews requirement text; the leaderboard scores citations only.

description: rules pick the regulations, then three Claude agents check each other on every shall-clause (strict reviewer + completeness auditor, adjudicator settles disagreements)
explain: The same checklist as devansh-llm-clause-filter picks the rulebooks (here 4 of the 55). Then three Claude agents check each other's work so that no applicable rule is missed. Agent A is a strict engineer: it keeps a rule only if it clearly applies to this product. Agent B is a completeness auditor: it keeps every rule that could apply and only drops clear misses. When A and B disagree, agent C, a senior adjudicator, reads the rule and both verdicts and makes the final call. Rules both keep are handed in, rules both drop are left out. Its weakness: the checklist was written while looking at this practice product.
explain_technical:
1. Regulation selection: `regselect` `combined` (about 35 hand-written regex rules + supersession and vehicle-category filters), identical to devansh-llm-clause-filter.
2. Candidates: every clause of the selected regulations in `data-ingestion/clauses` matching `\b(shall|must)\b`.
3. Multi-agent review (`classify.classify_multi`), all `claude-opus-5-5` with structured JSON output, batches of 40 clauses (25 for the adjudicator), 6 parallel requests, cached per batch:
- Agent A, strict applicability (the single-agent prompt, effort medium);
- Agent B, completeness auditor ("answer true unless clearly not applicable", effort medium);
- Agent C, adjudicator (effort high), only for clauses where A and B disagree, sees both verdicts. Final: A = B -> that verdict; A != B -> C's verdict. Agreement counts are in `outputs/review-report.json`.
4. Output: every kept clause as one requirement (clause text, first page, normalised paragraph); no size cut.
risk_flags: regulation rules written by looking at the dev product; reviewer prompts give lighting examples (headlamps, direction indicators) seen in the dev domain
risk_notes: Same selection as devansh-llm-clause-filter; the multi-agent review adds recall but no new dev tuning.

description: Claude writes regex patterns from the spec to pick the regulations, then one Claude agent keeps or drops each shall-clause
explain: Nothing is hand-written for the product. Claude reads only the product description (not the list of rulebooks, not the answers) and writes search patterns for its functions and parts, like "stop lamp" or "retro-reflect". Those patterns are searched in the title and scope of all 55 rulebooks; every rulebook that matches is picked, and older rulebooks replaced by newer ones are dropped. Then one Claude agent reads every rule that says something "shall" be done in the picked rulebooks and answers yes or no for this product. Its weakness: the patterns also catch a few rulebooks that do not apply, so the agent must reject their rules.
explain_technical:
1. Regulation selection: `regselect` `llm_regex`: `claude-opus-5-5` gets only `spec.md` and returns 6-20 case-insensitive regexes for the product's functions, components, installation and electronics (generic words forbidden); invalid regexes are dropped; each regulation whose title + paragraph 1 scope matches any pattern is selected; then the supersession and vehicle-category filters. Cached per spec in `devansh-toolkit/.cache`.
2. Candidates: every clause of the selected regulations in `data-ingestion/clauses` matching `\b(shall|must)\b`.
3. Classifier: single agent, `claude-opus-5-5` effort medium, structured output, batches of 40, cached per batch (the devansh-llm-clause-filter prompt).
4. Output: every kept clause as one requirement; no size cut.
risk_flags: classifier prompt gives lighting examples (headlamps, direction indicators) seen in the dev domain
risk_notes: Regulation selection is generated per spec by the LLM (no hand-written product rules), so it should transfer better than the rules-based variants; the regex prompt was not tuned against dev scores.

description: Exhaustive clause assessment with Haiku and independent Sonnet verification
explain: The method reads a product specification and checks each supplied regulation clause. Claude Haiku decides whether each assigned clause applies and can look up other clauses for context. Claude Sonnet independently checks proposed requirements before they are included. The output contains requirements with citations, plus separate diagnostic and cost reports. Its main weaknesses are incorrect applicability decisions, uncertain source text, and unresolved or failed batches.
explain_technical:
1. Read all 26,769 records from the base-regulation clause JSONs; never read expected.json during generation.
2. Partition consecutive records into batches of up to 12 / 14,000 characters, with up to 24,000 characters of initial context; use 10 concurrent workers.
3. Assess with claude-haiku-5-5 and verify with claude-sonnet-5-5. Each agent may use native search/read tools for up to 4 rounds / 8 calls. Retry failed batches twice.
4. Require evidence and restrict proposals to their assigned clauses; retain supported requirements without deduplication. No embeddings or database are used.
5. Export schema-compatible requirements; this saved run covers 26,709 of 26,769 records, with 1,058 assessments still needing context.
6. Rebenchmark on 2026-10-24: page F2 0.543478, clause F2 0.287081, regulation F2 0.800000. Page/regulation scores are unchanged; clause F2 is newly reported by the updated evaluator.
7. Overfit risk: medium; only the rear-lamp dev case has been evaluated. Parsing and examples were checked against dev inputs; no gold data is used by the generation pipeline.
risk_flags: Clause parsing and prompt examples were inspected using the rear-lamp development case; no score-based parameter sweep.
risk_notes: Only one labelled case has been evaluated. Models and concurrency were selected for cost/runtime. Production code does not read expected.json. This saved run has incomplete coverage; all scores are development citation metrics, not semantic correctness.

description: Claude writes regex patterns from the spec to pick the regulations, then one Claude agent with a product-neutral prompt judges every clause (no shall filter)
explain: Built to work on any product, not just the rear lamp. Claude reads only the product description and writes search patterns for its functions and parts; every rulebook whose title and scope match is picked (older rulebooks replaced by newer ones are dropped). Its weakness: it reads two to three times more rules, so it costs more, and it can still keep rules from rulebooks that matched by accident.

1. Regulation selection: `regselect` `llm_regex`: `claude-opus-5-5` sees only `spec.md` and returns 6-20 case-insensitive regexes (generic words forbidden); a regulation is selected when any pattern matches its title or paragraph 1 scope; then supersession and vehicle-category filters. description: Fixed clause catalogue + shared Gemini embeddings, exhaustive scoped assessment, independent Claude verification
explain: The input is a product specification and the fixed set of regulation texts. The program reuses the team's saved numerical descriptions of the source passages and organizes the passages with their surrounding rules. Claude first checks which regulations may apply, then reads every clause in those regulations and proposes requirements with source quotes. A separate pass checks each proposal before it enters the output, while uncertain decisions remain visible. The main weakness is that the initial regulation selection and the text extracted from tables can still be wrong or incomplete.
explain_technical:
1. Shared clause JSON and `gemini-embedding-2-preview` vectors, 26,769 rows × 768 dimensions; validate all citation metadata, normalize vectors and hash inputs.
2. Build source-only ancestor/reference catalogue; lexical eight-seed document similarity and RRF k60 prioritize work without removing clauses.
3. `claude-sonnet-5-5` quotes every regulation's scope decision; include uncertain regulations. No fixed regulation allowlist.
4. Assess all selected clauses, no page cap or cross-encoder; 24 clauses / 60,000 target characters per batch, four concurrent requests.
5. Independently verify proposals against complete source/context; retain only supported requirements, with full decision and budget audit.
6. Same frozen inference rules on development and unseen specifications (only a budget-reserve CLI was added before scoring); record scores after generation. High overfit risk because the architectural revision was informed by earlier development results.
7. Final development: page F2 0.842619, clause F2 0.628971, regulation F2 0.952381; 412 exported requirements. Held-out clause recall 0.701754, 508 requirements; Robust 0.772187. Citation scores do not establish semantic correctness. Both cases retain unresolved decisions, with no final budget-limited gaps.
risk_flags: Architecture revised after observing the previous SPLADE/dense development run: remove page cap and cross-encoder selection; use exhaustive selected-regulation clause assessment. No new threshold or model sweep against this run.
risk_notes: No product-specific regulation allowlist or keyword rules. The fixed source catalogue contains source clauses, not gold requirements. The held-out specification is passed through the same frozen inference rules without tuning; its gold is read only by the benchmark. The semantic priority uses existing document vectors seeded by lexical source matches, not a Gemini query encoder. New end-to-end results cannot isolate an embedding-only gain. Development page F2 improves to 0.842619 and clause F2 to 0.628971, but unseen clause recall is only 0.701754. The large output and unresolved applicability decisions remain material risks. No post-score tuning.

description: Agentic per-regulation scope screening followed by complete clause analysis
explain: One Opus agent inspects each regulation to decide whether it could apply to the product. It starts with the regulation's scope and first clauses, and can search or continue reading before deciding. Regulations it selects or remains unsure about are kept. Sonnet agents then read every clause in those regulations and propose applicable requirements, followed by a separate Sonnet verification pass. A mistaken clear rejection can still hide an applicable regulation.
explain_technical:
1. Load all 26,769 parsed clauses in the currently indexed 56 base regulation/version groups. Read the product specification only; never read expected answers. No embeddings, vector database, Gemini API, fixed regulation list, or case-specific keywords.
2. Run one `claude-opus-5-5` screening conversation per regulation, 10 concurrently. Supply the title, identifiable scope, first 8 clauses, and at most 40,000 initial characters. Native tools are regulation-local sequential reading, lexical search, and arbitrary chunked clause reading. Budgets: 6 rounds, 12 calls; retry failed tasks twice.
3. Retain `select` and `uncertain` decisions. Also retain failed screening tasks while recording the error. Remove only `reject` decisions. Save exact specification evidence, confidence, topics, API turns and tool traces.
4. Fully assess all retained clauses with `claude-sonnet-5-5`, 10 workers, batches of at most 12 clauses/14,000 target characters, 24,000 context characters, and 4 rounds/8 cross-corpus lexical tool calls. Each clause is assigned once and can emit only its own obligations.
5. Verify proposed requirements independently with `claude-sonnet-5-5`; keep supported candidates, retain duplicates, and validate the official schema. Save predictions, screening, diagnostics and estimated costs separately.
6. Dev run `37ec3cfc2ef94836ade4be35cadc585d`: 9 regulations, 5,107 assessed clauses, 616 exported requirements, estimated cost $21.7112. Page P/R/F1/F2 = 0.3355/0.9623/0.4976/0.7005; clause = 0.1412/0.6860/0.2341/0.3871; regulation = 0.4444/1.0000/0.6154/0.8000. No holdout score and no dev tuning. Medium overfitting risk; the dominant generalization risk is a regulation-level screening false negative, while the observed dev weakness is low clause precision.
risk_notes: No embeddings or case-specific regulation filters. A screening false negative can remove an entire relevant regulation; uncertain and failed screens are therefore included. Dev run has high recall but low precision. No holdout run and no score-driven tuning.

description: Agentic vector discovery and scope-confirmed regulation scans
explain: Claude reads the product specification and chooses several searches for relevant rules. Each search proposes distinct candidate regulations from our local database. Claude inspects promising candidates and explicitly chooses which regulations deserve a full scan. Workers check every clause in those selected regulations, followed by independent verification. A regulation missed during search or rejected during inspection will not be assessed.
explain_technical:
1. Read the shared LanceDB `clauses` table (26,769 records, 56 regulation/version groups in the current corpus). Validate base versions against the challenge index; never read answer keys.
2. `claude-sonnet-5-5` chooses adaptive native tool searches: at least 4 distinct queries, at most 18 total search/inspection calls over 12 rounds per planning attempt. Embed plain query text using the same shared REST helper as clause ingestion, with `gemini-embedding-2-preview` and 768 dimensions. Validate the shared database model manifest first; no embedding-model fallback.
3. For every query, run exact cosine comparison against all 26,769 clauses and group results into distinct regulation/version candidates. Rank each regulation by the average of its 3 strongest clause similarities and return the top 12 candidates per query. Search results do not automatically enter the scan.

Workers have lexical search/read context tools, up to 4 rounds/8 calls, and may emit only their assigned clauses. Retry failed batches twice.
5. Independently verify proposed requirements using `claude-sonnet-5-5` and the same context tools. Only supported candidates enter predictions; no requirement deduplication. Uncertain/irrelevant assessments are not independently reassessed.
6. Validate the official output schema. Save separate predictions, diagnostics, retrieval trace, Claude cost estimate, and unpriced Gemini request counts. Output size depends on supported candidates and must meet official limits. Spec text only; no product image.
7. Dev run `0d47e3ab48644982884fa2b10ba142e9`: 5 searches, 19 discovered candidates, 6 selected regulations, 2,746 assessed clauses, 571 ...

description: devansh-llm-clause-filter-writer, then a product-neutral verifier drops non-obligations and near-duplicate requirements (for the one-to-one requirement judge)
explain: This is the current best approach plus a final check. First the checklist picks the rulebooks, Claude keeps the rules that apply, and a writer turns each rule into single, clearly worded obligations. Then a second Claude reviewer reads the finished list like an engineer would before handing it to a supplier: it removes items that are not real obligations for this product (definitions, steps of a lab test procedure, paperwork done by the authorities, features the product does not have) and removes repeats. The scoring robot pairs each of our requirements with at most one expert requirement, so every extra or repeated item counts against us; this check is meant to cut those. Its risk: it may also drop a few real obligations.
explain_technical:
1. Input: `devansh-llm-clause-filter-writer` predictions (rules selection, opus 5.5 clause filter on shall-clauses, strict writer splitting clauses into single obligations).
2. Dedupe (`refine.dedupe`): drop a requirement whose normalised text repeats one already kept in the same regulation, or whose word set has Jaccard >= 0.9 with one kept from the same paragraph (one-to-one matching: repeats can only be false positives).
3. Verifier (`refine.verify`): `claude-opus-5-5`, effort medium, structured output `{id, keep}`, batches of 30 sorted by regulation and page so neighbours are judged together; product-neutral drop rules (missing function / variant, definition or bare condition, authority procedure, test-procedure step, repeat). Undecided items are kept.
4. Scored with `bench.py` (citations) and `req_judge.py` (requirement level, the platform's main score) on dev-rear-lamp and holdout-acpe; adopt only if requirement F2 improves on both.
risk_flags: inherits devansh-llm-clause-filter-writer: regulation rules and writer style rules written while looking at the dev case; the verifier's drop categories (test-procedure steps, authority duties, definitions, repeats) were chosen after the dev error analysis showed most unmatched requirements come from unlisted paragraphs
risk_notes: No thresholds or sizes fitted; the verifier prompt names no product. Judged on the unseen holdout-acpe case as well.

explain: Before choosing any rules, Claude studies the product the way an engineer would: it reads the description AND the exploded-view drawing. Candidates `shall+implicit`: shall / must clauses plus clauses matching an implicit-obligation pattern (comparisons like "not less than", "is not permitted", "provided that", test instructions, "Label: value" lines, values with units). description: profile-faithful v2: same pipeline (profile from spec + image, Claude judges shall + implicit clauses, faithful writer, 1-5 ranker) minus clauses cited at Table / Figure / Appendix labels, plus a rest
explain: The same steps as our best version (Claude studies the product description and drawing, picks the rules that apply, rewrites each rule into single obligations, and does a final 1-5 check), with two clean-ups aimed at fewer wrong answers. First, it no longer turns value tables, figures and appendices into requirements: in the regulations, a numbered paragraph says "the lamp shall meet the values in Table 7", and the experts list that paragraph, not every cell of the table. Second, at the end Claude looks for obligations that appear twice in the list (for example a limit stated in the main text and again in an annex) and keeps only one copy, because each expert requirement can be matched only once. Every answer is generated fresh for this version; nothing is reused from earlier runs. Main weakness: if experts for a future product do cite a table, those requirements are now missing.

1. Fresh LLM cache: `LLM_CACHE_DIR=approaches/experiments/devansh-profile-faithful-v2/.cache` (git-ignored); all Claude answers (profile, classifier, writer, ranker, restatement merge) are generated for this run only.
2. `profile.build_profile` (`claude-opus-5-5`, effort high) from spec.md + exploded-view image, appended to the spec.
3. Regulation selection `combined` (keyword rules + supersession + category filters) on the ORIGINAL spec.

5. Clause classifier (opus 5.5, effort medium) with the profile-augmented spec; faithful writer (effort medium).
6. `refine --mode rank --drop-at-or-below 1` (exact / near-text dedupe, drop only rating 1, cut-off inherited).

NEW `refine --merge-restatements`: per regulation (batches of up to 150 items, page order), Claude returns groups of items that state exactly the same obligation (same subject, condition, value); conservative rules exclude different values / categories / voltage systems, pointer vs detailed test text, and halves of one clause. From each group the copy at a numbered main-text paragraph (else the earliest page) is kept.
